name: RepresentUs Education Fund (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the US's people, whose government the work defends and reforms (the reform branches' people are in the US places that adopted ranked-choice voting or redistricting commissions); the spillover abroad (a side-effect share of the US value) isn't assigned to countries.
summary: The RepresentUs Education Fund, the 501(c)(3) of the US anti-corruption and democracy-reform group RepresentUs (Represent.Us itself is a 501(c)(4), and gifts to it aren't tax-deductible, so this models the Education Fund only), spent $7.8 million in 2024 on national videos and social media about corruption and threats to democracy, education and volunteer outreach behind state and local ballot measures, research, the American Democracy Summit and grants to Represent.Us for campaign outreach. Four branches, each its share of the money behind what its field or movement achieves: its {{row:rcv_attribution_share_shared}} share of the resources behind the ranked-choice voting movement (its volunteers' time counted with the others'), which puts about 1.4 million more Americans a year under ranked ballots (about a third of the result); its 3% share of the movement that moved 79 million Americans' maps to redistricting commissions since 2008 (about a quarter); its other reforms (anti-corruption laws, money in politics, ethics), judged a quarter as effective per dollar as the redistricting movement (about a fifth); and its direct work's small share of the US pro-democracy field's yearly cut in the chance that the US falls to a hybrid regime before 2030 (about a fifth). With its next dollar at {{row:marginal_vs_past_average}} of the average, it comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars; the result is mostly judgment (the years a win counts, how much a voting reform changes how well people are governed, the split of its spending between the branches), and all four branches are discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: The Education Fund's own spending in calendar 2024 on its four programme columns, with its management and fundraising, from its audited statements. Represent.Us, the 501(c)(4), is left out: gifts to it aren't tax-deductible; the Fund's grant to it is counted as the work it funds. The programme is split four ways for the branches: direct work against a slide, ranked-choice voting, redistricting reform, and other reforms.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: Who the work reaches: everyone governed by US democracy (the slide branch), the people newly under ranked-choice voting each year of the movement's work, and the people in the states that moved their maps to commissions since 2008.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the work changes: the chance that US democracy slides to a hybrid regime, valued by the income a slide would cost as it builds up; and reforms within the democracy (ranked-choice voting, fair maps, then anti-corruption, money in politics and ethics rules), valued as a share of democracy's income gain. Each counts the whole field's or movement's effect; the Education Fund's share is in the adjustments.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Each branch's own discounts for trust in the estimate, the Education Fund's share of its field's resources, delivery and missing data; the canonical rows are their averages, for reading only.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Share of the programme acting on a democratic slide directly
rows.explainer: Work as direct as Protect Democracy's (the field's 'direct' dollar, @democracy.field_direct_share): in 2024 the AI-deepfake PSA warning voters in seven swing states about false information on when and where to vote (6.6 million paid views, 2024 Impact Report p. 5), the Election Protection education platform it launched in 2023 (note 1), and its education about corrupt authoritarianism (Form 990, Part III); the 2025 pivot to pressing Congress on checks on the executive came after the modelled year. Most of the programme is reform education and the ballot campaigns behind it, counted in the three reform branches only. Judged 20% (10% to 40%), under Common Cause's 35% because RepresentUs runs no hotline, election-official work or litigation.

rows.label: Share of the reform work (all but the direct work) on ranked-choice voting
rows.explainer: The 2024 Impact Report (p. 6) lists 21 campaigns: eight to pass ranked-choice voting and voting reform (Oregon, Nevada, Washington DC, Richmond CA, Connecticut, Arizona, Colorado, Idaho), and three of its five 'democracy defense' campaigns defended ranked-choice voting or open primaries (Alaska's repeal measure, Arizona's four constitutional measures, Missouri's Amendment 7); two were on anti-corruption (Maine, Ann Arbor) and two on gerrymandering (Los Angeles, Ohio). Its largest restricted balance at the end of 2024 is for 'Ranked Choice Voting Campaigns' ($837,546, note 7). Campaigns are one part of the reform work beside its national education on corruption, so judged 45% (25% to 65%) of the reform work, short of the campaign count's half.

rows.label: Share of the reform work (all but the direct work) on redistricting commissions
rows.explainer: Two of the 21 campaigns of 2024 were against gerrymandering: Los Angeles's Measure DD (an independent city redistricting commission, passed with 75%) and Ohio's Issue 1 (lost), 2024 Impact Report pp. 6 and 11; 'Anti Gerrymandering' holds $390,531 of the restricted balance (note 7), and its 2025 work continued with research and partner outreach on anti-gerrymandering. Judged 12% (5% to 25%) of the reform work, a little above the campaign count's 10% for the restricted money.

rows.label: Long-run income gain from staying a democracy (share of GDP per person)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/democracy.json): Acemoglu et al. (2019)'s long-run income effect of democracy, read by every model of work against a US slide.

rows.label: Share of democracy's income gain a slide to a hybrid regime would lose
rows.explainer: The shared figure: a slide to a hybrid regime loses part of democracy's gain, not all of it.

rows.label: Long-run income loss of a slide per person per year, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: The income a slide would cost each person each year once it had built up, on the site's log scale.

rows.label: Chance the US falls to a hybrid regime before 2030
rows.explainer: The shared forecast (facts/democracy.json), the stake for every model of work against a US slide.

rows.label: Relative cut in that chance from one year of the whole US pro-democracy field's work
rows.explainer: The shared figure for the whole field's yearly effect; the Education Fund's share of the field is in the adjustments.

rows.label: Chance a year of the field's work averts a slide
rows.explainer: The chance removed, counted at its expected value as every model of the field does (the field's work is thousands of cases and campaigns, not one bet).

rows.label: Years from the work until a slide it averts would have come
rows.explainer: Its work year is calendar 2024: the forecast counts the Economist's reports published before 2030; those for 2024 and 2025 showed no slide, so a slide averted would on average have come in 2027, three years after 2024's work (2 to 5).

rows.label: Discount for the wait (slide branch)
rows.explainer: The wait until the slide would have come, at the shared discount rate.

rows.label: Years over which democracy's income effect builds up
rows.explainer: The shared build-up (facts/democracy.json): a slide's loss and a reform's gain both build up over about 25 years.

rows.label: Rate for the slide's loss: the shared discount rate plus the reversal hazard
rows.explainer: A slide, once it happens, may be undone (the shared reversal rate), so the loss averted counts at the discount rate plus that hazard.

rows.label: Discounted years of the full loss averted by putting a slide off
rows.formula: (1 - (1 + bs_rate) ^ (0 - years_of_impact)) * (1 - (1 + bs_rate) ^ (0 - ramp_years)) / (ln(1 + bs_rate) * ln(1 + bs_rate) * ramp_years) * bs_wait_discount
rows.explainer: The shifted ramp of the family's 'Democracy and governance' section: a slide put off by the years counted moves its whole build-up, worth this many full-loss years after the wait.

rows.label: Income loss averted by a year of the field's work, units of value (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Everyone in the US × the loss per person-year × the chance a year of the field removes × the discounted years, valued at the shared value of a doubled income.

rows.label: Income gained per person-year once the effect is fully built, ln(consumption) (RCV branch)
rows.explainer: Ranked-choice voting's share (@democracy.rcv_gain_share, 2%, 0.3% to 6%) of the long-run income gain of becoming a democracy (@democracy.democratization_gdp_gain, 21%): the family's rule for a reform within a democracy. The build-up is in rcv_discounted_years.

rows.label: Years from the win until ranked ballots are first used
rows.explainer: The shared figure: about a year and a half (1 to 3).

rows.label: Discount for the wait (RCV branch)
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discount rate plus repeal hazard (RCV branch)
rows.explainer: The shared rate plus the shared yearly chance a won electoral reform is repealed or banned (@democracy.electoral_reform_repeal_rate, 3%, its anchor the record of US ranked-choice repeals and state bans): repeal is a separate question from the years counted (the family's rule).

rows.label: Discounted full-effect years a won reform counts (RCV branch, its ramp brought forward)
rows.formula: (1 - (1 + rcv_rate) ^ (0 - years_of_impact)) * (1 - (1 + rcv_rate) ^ (0 - ramp_years)) / (ln(1 + rcv_rate) * ln(1 + rcv_rate) * ramp_years) * rcv_wait_discount
rows.explainer: The family's shifted ramp: the effect builds over ramp_years from first use, and bringing the reform forward by years_of_impact moves the whole ramp earlier; present value at the shared rate plus the repeal hazard, times the wait.

rows.label: Units of value per year of the movement's work (RCV branch, before adjustments)
rows.explainer: People newly covered × the income gained × the value of a log point × the discounted full-effect years.

rows.label: Share of democracy's income gain that an independent redistricting commission brings
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/democracy.json): share of democracy's income gain that an independent redistricting commission brings.

rows.label: Income gained per person-year once the effect is fully built, ln(consumption) (redistricting branch)
rows.explainer: The reform's share of democracy's long-run income gain, per person-year, on the log scale.

rows.label: Years from a year's work until a commission's first maps are used
rows.explainer: Our judgment: a campaign takes about a year to win and a commission first draws after the next census or soon after it is set up (California 2008 to 2011 maps, Michigan and Colorado 2018 to 2021, Ohio 2015 to 2021), measured from calendar 2024's work: {{row:maps_years_until_effect}} years ({{range:maps_years_until_effect}}).

rows.label: Discount for the wait (redistricting branch)
rows.explainer: The wait until the first commission maps, at the shared discount rate.

rows.label: Discount rate plus repeal hazard (redistricting branch)
rows.explainer: Won reforms of how elections work are often undone (the shared repeal rate): Missouri's 2018 reform was repealed in 2020, Utah's legislature reversed much of Proposition 4, and California's 2025 Proposition 50 set the commission's congressional map aside until 2030.

rows.label: Discounted full-effect years a won commission counts (its ramp brought forward)
rows.formula: (1 - (1 + maps_rate) ^ (0 - years_of_impact)) * (1 - (1 + maps_rate) ^ (0 - ramp_years)) / (ln(1 + maps_rate) * ln(1 + maps_rate) * ramp_years) * maps_wait_discount
rows.explainer: The shifted ramp: the reform brought forward by the years counted moves its whole build-up, at the discount rate plus the repeal hazard, after the wait.

rows.label: Units of value per year of the redistricting movement's work (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: People newly under a commission per year × the gain per person-year × the discounted years, valued at the shared value of a doubled income.

rows.label: A dollar of the other reform work against a dollar of the redistricting movement
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/democracy.json): a dollar of other reform work (voting access, money in politics, ethics, media) against a dollar of the redistricting movement.

rows.label: Units of value per year of reform work the size of the redistricting movement, other reforms (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The redistricting movement's yearly value scaled by the other reforms' relative effect: the Education Fund's share is its spending on them over that movement's resources (oth_attribution_share).

rows.label: Years a won reform or postponed slide counts
rows.explainer: The shared number of years a won reform (or a slide put off) counts before it would have come anyway (docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Whole field's resources as a multiple of its institutional philanthropy
rows.explainer: The shared figure: 501(c)(4) money, individual donors and pro bono work on top of foundations' grants.

rows.label: Share of the field doing direct work against a slide
rows.explainer: The shared figure: litigation, election protection, checks on power and election-official support, against the rest of the field.

rows.label: Effect of an indirect dollar on a slide, relative to a direct dollar
rows.explainer: The shared figure, weighting the field's indirect dollars in its resources.

rows.label: The pro-democracy field's resources in the year, in direct-work dollars of 2024
rows.explainer: Institutional philanthropy for US democracy (2021-2022 dollars) × the whole field's multiple of it, counted in direct-work dollars (the direct share plus the rest at its relative effect), in 2024 prices: the shared chain every model of work against a US slide uses.

rows.label: The Education Fund's share of the field's resources against a slide
rows.explainer: Its 2024 spending on direct work over the field's direct-work dollars (Convention 2: share of resources, never an equal split): about 0.06%. Its reform work counts in the three reform branches only.

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with money, work or budgets it brings in
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): governments' budgets and enforcement, companies' compliance, the use others make of research. The charity is credited this share of the good done with them, net of their cost; the rest stays with those who paid or did the work. Fixed.

rows.label: Share of credit used: the Education Fund's share of the field's resources against a slide
rows.explainer: The share among those who paid for or did the same work, times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out or adopt the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.explainer: The shared figure: the cross-country income effect of democracy applied to the US.

rows.label: Share of the slide outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The field's cut is already against a world without its work, and the years counted say the slide would come some day: nothing more to take off.

rows.label: Share of the slide outcome enforced
rows.explainer: A slide averted isn't a law to enforce: 1.

rows.explainer: No measured outcome for the Education Fund's effect on the chance of a slide: the shared discount (Convention 12).

source.title: RepresentUs, 2024 Impact Report (December 2024; covers Represent.Us and the Education Fund together)
source.page: p. 7 (In 2024, we activated thousands of advocates)
source.quote: 6.7 MILLION TEXTS AND CALLS MADE BY DEDICATED VOLUNTEERS

rows.explainer: Its volunteers' outreach for the 2024 ballot campaigns, both arms together (the Fund's staff train and run the volunteer network; its grant to Represent.Us pays for the texting and calling): unpaid time behind the same wins, a resource of others (Convention 2).

rows.label: Volunteer time per text or call
rows.explainer: Peer-to-peer texting tools send a message in a few seconds and a phone-bank call, most of them unanswered, takes a few minutes; RepresentUs's contacts are mostly texts (2 million texts in Arizona alone in 2024, and 600,000 texts to 100,000 calls in 2025, 2025 Year in Review p. 7). Six texts at about 5 seconds and one call at about 3 minutes average about 30 seconds a contact: judged 0.01 hours (0.003 to 0.03), training and meetings included.

rows.label: Value of the volunteers' time, 2024
rows.explainer: At the site's US value of a volunteer hour (@united_states.volunteer_hour_value_2024): about $2.3 million. The contacts were for the 2024 ballot measures, so it is split over the three reform branches by the reform work's shares, and none goes to the slide branch.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, RCV branch
rows.explainer: The shared figure (0.5, 0.25 to 0.85): rcv_gain_share is the gain if it is real; this is the doubt that single-winner ranked-choice voting changes what governments decide at all.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway, RCV branch
rows.explainer: 1: $win_years_counted already says the reforms would have come some day (Convention 5).

rows.label: Share of a full switch that the places counted get, RCV branch
rows.explainer: The shared figures, about 44%: the local part (@democracy.rcv_local_coverage, 68%) × the share of a full switch a city's own elections bring (@democracy.local_offices_weight, 50%), plus the state and federal part (@democracy.rcv_state_federal_coverage, 10%); weighted by the people added: New York City uses ranked ballots for its primaries and special elections, Maine for primaries and federal races, Hawaii only for special elections, cities for their own offices.

rows.label: The Education Fund's share of the ranked-choice movement's resources
rows.explainer: Its 2024 spending on ranked-choice voting (about $2.8 million) over the whole movement's average yearly spending in 2016-2025 (@democracy.us_rcv_movement_resources_per_year, $19 million in 2024 dollars, ballot campaigns, FairVote and RepresentUs included; Convention 2), plus its own volunteers' time on this work (the shared figure counts money): about {{row:rcv_attribution_share_shared}}. A 2024 year of its work against an average movement year, so the result per dollar is the movement's wins per dollar spent. 2024 was a year of large ballot spending, most of it on statewide measures that failed (all but Alaska's defence; Washington DC's Initiative 83 passed), which is why the average year is the base, not 2024's record.

rows.explainer: The share among those who paid for or did the same work, times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out or adopt the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.explainer: The shared figure for a won voting-method reform; for maps, the 2025 mid-decade redistricting in Texas and the answers it provoked elsewhere (California's Proposition 50) show the same pattern of counter-measures.

rows.label: Redistricting side effects, summed
rows.explainer: The redistricting branch's side effects, each weighted by the side-effect slider.

rows.label: The Education Fund's other reform spending over the redistricting movement's resources
rows.explainer: Its 2024 spending on the other reforms over the redistricting movement's yearly resources, the scale oth_relative_effect is set against, plus its own volunteers' time on this work: about {{row:oth_attribution_share_shared}}.

rows.label: Share of credit used: the Education Fund's other reform spending over the redistricting movement's resources
rows.explainer: The share among those who paid for or did the same work, times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out or adopt the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, other-reforms branch
rows.explainer: The same trust in the chain as the redistricting branch it is scaled from; the weaker evidence for these reforms is in oth_relative_effect, not counted twice.

rows.label: Share of the other reforms' outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The years counted already say the reforms would have come some day (Convention 5).

rows.label: Share of the other reforms' effect delivered
rows.explainer: oth_relative_effect compares a dollar of this work with a dollar of the redistricting movement as delivered, so the redistricting wins' delivered share carries over here; it isn't a claim that voting-access or money-in-politics reforms are delivered like commissions.

rows.label: Missing-data discount, other-reforms branch
rows.explainer: No measured outcome: the shared discount (Convention 12).

rows.label: All adjustments, other-reforms branch
rows.explainer: The product of the other-reforms branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Side effect: fairer elections valued beyond income, other-reforms branch
rows.explainer: The shared figure for a won reform of how elections work, read as in the redistricting branch.

rows.label: Side effect: counter-measures, other-reforms branch
rows.explainer: The shared figure: access reforms provoke restrictions elsewhere as voting-method reforms provoke bans.

rows.label: Other-reforms side effects, summed
